readings.c1s1:
¶
'''underivedness''' (un-dẹ̄-rī′ved-nes), ''n.'' The character or state of being underived. ''Mind'', XI. 39.

'''underjawed''' (un′dėr-jâd), ''a.'' Having a prominent or heavy under jaw. ''Athenæum'', No. 3300, p. 128. [Rare.]

'''underjoint†''' (un-dėr-join′), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''underjoinen''; < ''under'' + ''join''.] To subjoin. ''Wyclif'', Prol. to Psalms, p. 737.

'''underkeep†''' (un-dėr-kēp′), ''v. t.'' To keep under; subdue. ''Spenser'', F. Q., III. vii. 33.

'''under-kind''' (un′dėr-kīnd), ''n.'' A lower or inferior kind or class. ''Dryden'', An Evening’s Love, i. 1.

'''under-king''' (un′dėr-king), ''n.'' [< ME. ''underking'', < AS. ''undercyning'', ''underkining''; as < ''under'' + ''king''<sup>1</sup>.] An inferior or subordinate king.

'''under-kingdom''' (un′dėr-king″dum), ''n.'' The kingdom of an under-king. ''Tennyson'', Merlin and Vivien.

'''underlay''' (un-dėr-lā′), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''underlaid'', ppr. ''underlaying''. [< ME. ''underleyan'', < AS. ''underlecgan'' (= OHG. ''untarleccan'', MHG. G. ''unterlegen''), lay under; as ''under'' + ''lay''<sup>1</sup>.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To lay beneath; put under; specifically, in ''printing'', to reinforce with underlays.—'''2†.''' To support by laying something under.
{{smaller block|<poem>Our souls have trod awry in all men’s sight;
We’ll ''under-lay'' ’em, till they go upright.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'' (''and another''), Love’s Cure, v. 3.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' In ''mining'', to incline from the perpendicular; hade: said of a vein. See the noun.
readings.c1s4:
¶
'''underlie''' (un′dėr-lī), ''n.'' [< ''underlie'', ''v.''] In ''mining'', same as ''underlay'', 1.

'''under-life''' (un′dėr-līf), ''n.'' Life below the surface; hence, a way of living apart and different from the life open to the common knowledge or view. ''Harper’s Mag.'', LXXVI. 753. [Rare.]

'''underline''' (un-dėr-līn′), ''v. t.'' '''1.''' To mark underneath or below with a line; underscore: as, to ''underline'' words in a letter.—'''2†.''' To influence secretly.
readings.c2s1:
{{smaller block|By mere chance, . . . though ''underlined'' with a providence, they had a full sight of the infanta.
{{right|''Sir H. Wotton'', Reliquiæ, p. 215.}}}}

¶
'''underline''' (un′dėr-līn), ''n.'' The advance announcement of the production of a play, placed under any theatrical advertisement of a regular performance.

'''underlinen''' (un′dėr-lin″en), ''n.'' Undergarments of linen; hence, such garments in general, especially those of cotton, or, more rarely, of silk, as distinguished from knitted or flannel underclothes.

'''underling''' (un′dėr-ling), ''n.'' [< ME. ''underling'', ''onderling''; < ''under'' + ''-ling''<sup>1</sup>.] One who is subordinate to another, especially in some mean or servile capacity; hence, a mean, sorry fellow.
{{smaller block|Extorcions and despit of youre ''underlynges'' is dampnable.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Parson’s Tale.}}
<poem>The fault . . . is
. . . in ourselves, that we are ''underlings''.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', J. C., i. 2. 141.}}}}

'''underlock''' (un′dėr-lok), ''n.'' A lock of wool hanging under the belly of a sheep. ''Imp. Dict.''

'''underlooker''', ''n.'' See ''underviewer''.

'''underly''' (un′dėr-li), ''a.'' [< ''under'' + ''-ly''<sup>1</sup>.] Poor; inferior. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]

'''underlying''' (un-dėr-lī′ing), ''p. a.'' Lying beneath or under; supporting; fundamental: as, ''underlying'' principles; specifically, in ''geol.'', noting a formation, rocks, or strata lying below others.

'''underman''' (un-dėr-man′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''undermanned'', ppr. ''undermanning''. To furnish with an insufficient number of men. ''Nature'', XLI. 520.
readings.c2s2:
¶
'''undermasted''' (un-dėr-mȧs′ted), ''a.'' Inadequately or insufficiently masted: noting a ship when the masts are either too small or too short, so that she cannot spread the sail necessary to give her the speed of which she might be capable.

'''undermatch†''' (un′dėr-mach), ''n.'' One unequal or inferior to some one else. ''Fuller'', Worthies, II. 589.

'''undermeal†''' (un′dėr-mēl), ''n.'' [< ME. ''undermele'', ''undermel'', < AS. ''undernmǣl'', morning, morning meal, < ''undern'', morning, + ''mǣl'', period, meal: see ''undern'' and ''meal''<sup>2</sup>.] '''1.''' The meal eaten at undern, the chief meal of the day.
{{smaller block|I think I am furnished for cather’ne pears, for one ''undermeal.''
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Bartholomew Fair, iv. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' The part or division of the day which included undern: originally the morning, later the afternoon.
{{smaller block|<poem>Ther walketh now the lymytour hymself
In ''undermeles'' and in morwenynges.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Wife of Bath’s Tale, l. 19.}}
''Undermele'', Postmeridies. {{right|''Prompt. Parv.'', p. 511.}}}}
'''3.''' An after-dinner sleep; a siesta taken in the afternoon.
{{smaller block|And, hold you content, this summer an ''vndermeale'' of an afternoone long doth not amisse to exercise the eyes withall.
{{right|''Nashe'', Pierce Penilesse, p. 57.}}}}

'''undermentioned''' (un′dėr-men″shọnd), ''a.'' Mentioned below or beneath; undernamed: as, ''undermentioned'' dates.
readings.c2s3:
¶
'''undermine''' (un-dėr-mīn′), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''underminen''; < ''under'' + ''mine''<sup>2</sup>.] '''1.''' To form a mine under; sap; render unstable by digging or wearing away the foundation of; make an excavation beneath, especially for the purpose of causing to fall, or of blowing up: as, to ''undermine'' a wall; a river ''undermines'' its banks.
{{smaller block|If Troy be not taken till these two ''undermine'' it, the walls will stand till they fall of themselves.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., ii. 3. 9.}}}}
'''2.''' Figuratively, to subvert by removing clandestinely the foundation of; injure by invisible, secret, or dishonorable means.
{{smaller block|<poem>Honours now are purchased by stealth
Of ''vndermining'' bribes.</poem>
{{right|''Times’ Whistle'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 44.}}
<poem>They . . .
Have hired me to ''undermine'' the duchess.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., i. 2. 98.}}}}
'''3.''' To injure, weaken, or destroy insidiously or indirectly; wear away; wear out; sap.
{{smaller block|The constitution became so ''undermined'' [by ostitis] that I deemed amputation of the thigh necessary.
{{right|''J. M. Carnochan'', Operative Surgery, p. 61.}}}}

'''undermine†''' (un′dėr-mīn), ''n.'' '''1.''' Same as ''mine''<sup>2</sup>, 2 (''a'').
{{smaller block|They put fire in the ''vndermines'', weening to haue cast downe the wall. {{right|''Hakluyt’s Voyages'', II. 86.}}}}
'''2.''' A cave. ''Holland'', Camden, p. 650.

'''underminer''' (un-dėr-mī′nėr), ''n.'' '''1.''' One who undermines, saps, or excavates. ''Shak.'', All’s Well, i. 1. 131.—'''2.''' Figuratively, one who clandestinely subverts or injures; one who secretly
readings.c3s1:
overthrows; a secret enemy: as, an ''underminer'' of the church.
{{smaller block|What talke I to them of immoralitie, that are the onely ''vnderminers'' of honour, & doo enuie anie man that is not sprung vp by base brokerye like themselues?
{{right|''Nashe'', Pierce Penilesse, p. 60.}}}}

'''underminister†''' (un-dėr-min′is-tėr), ''v. t.'' To minister to in a subordinate relation.

'''underministry''' (un′dėr-min″is-tri), ''n.'' A subservient or subordinate ministry. ''Jer. Taylor.''

'''undermirth†''' (un′dėr-mėrth), ''n.'' Mirth implying something indecent or with a hidden meaning. ''Shirley and Fletcher'', Coronation, Prol.

'''undermonied†''' (un-dėr-mun′id), ''a.'' Taken by corrupt means with money. ''Fuller.''

'''undermost''' (un′dėr-mōst), ''a.'' Lowest in place, rank, state, or condition. ''Boyle.''

'''undern''' (un′dėrn), ''n.'' [In mod. dial. use in numerous corrupt forms, ''aandorn'', ''oander'', ''oandurth'', ''omdorns'', ''ounder'', ''oneder'', ''aunder'', ''dondinner'', ''doundrins'', ''daundrin'', etc.; < ME. ''undern'', ''undorn'', ''undarn'', ''undren'', ''ondern'', ''ondre'', < AS. ''undern'', nine o’clock, morning, = OS. ''undorn'', ''undern'' = OHG. ''untarn'', MHG. ''undern'', G. dial. ''untern'', breakfast, supper, dinner, = Icel. ''undorn'', mid-forenoon, also mid-afternoon, = Goth. ''undaurni-'', in ''undaurni-mats'', a morning meal: lit. ‘intervening period,’ < AS. ''under'', etc., under: see ''under'', and cf. ''undermeal'', ''undertide'', ''undertime''.] '''1.''' Nine o’clock in the morning; the period from nine o’clock to noon; the canonical hour of terce. [Obsolete or prov. Eng. and Scotch.]
readings.c3s3:
''man'' (= OHG. ''untarneman'', MHG. ''undernemen'', G. ''unternehmen''), undertake, perceive, < ''under'', under, + ''niman'', take: see ''nim''. Cf. ''underfang'', ''underget'', ''undertake''.] '''1.''' To take; undertake.
{{smaller block|We beoth hider come and this fiht habbeth ''ondernome''.
{{right|''Layamon'', l. 26734.}}}}
'''2.''' To receive; feel; perceive.
{{smaller block|<poem>He the savour ''undernom''
Which that the roses and the lilies caste.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Second Nun’s Tale, l. 243.}}}}
'''3.''' To take up; reprove; reproach.
{{smaller block|Inpacient is he that wol nat ben ytaught ne ''undernome'' of his vice.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Parson’s Tale.}}
Who-so ''vndernymeth'' me here-of I hat hym dedly after.
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), v. 115.}}}}

'''undernote''' (un′dėr-nōt), ''n.'' A low or subdued note; an undertone.
{{smaller block|How every pause is filled with ''undernotes''.
{{right|''Shelley'', Prometheus Unbound, iv. 1.}}}}

'''undernoted''' (un′dėr-nō″ted), ''a.'' Noted below or beneath: as, the ''undernoted'' quantities.

'''undern-song†''', ''n.'' An office sung at undern, or nine o’clock in the morning. ''Rock.''

'''underntime†''', ''n.'' See ''undertime''.

'''underpart''' (un-dėr-pärt′), ''v. t.'' To divide (a part) and assign subordinate portions of it. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Then one part
Is ''under-parted'' to a couple of clerks.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Staple of News, i. 2.}}}}

To lie under or beneath; be situated under; specifically, in ''geol.'', to occupy a lower position than, or to pass beneath: said of stratified rocks over which other rocks are spread out. {{smaller|Thus the Triassic is, in some regions, underlain by the coal-measures, etc. A rock which underlies another is, ordinarily, the older of the two.}} —'''2.''' To be at the basis of; form the foundation of.
{{smaller block|''Underlying'' as it does the right organization of society, the law of equal freedom is of higher authority than all other laws. {{right|''H. Spencer'', Social Statics, p. 217.}}}}
'''3.''' To lie under, in a figurative sense; be subject to; be liable to answer, as a charge or a challenge.

And sall nocht mys the scurge and rod
Off the hie puissant and mychtie god.</poem>

I am not only willing but desirous to ''underlie'' the verdict even of Fame herself. {{right|''G. Harvey'', Four Letters, iii.}}

'''II.''' ''prep.'' Under; beneath.
{{smaller block|<poem>And so the stede fell ''vnder nethe'' hym dede.</poem>
{{right|''Generydes'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2498.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''Underneath'' this stone doth lie
As much beauty as could die.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Epigrams, cxxiv.}}}}

'''underniceness''' (un-dėr-nīs′nes), ''n.'' Deficient niceness, delicacy, or fastidiousness. ''Richardson'', Clarissa Harlowe, v. 8.

'''undernim†''', ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''undernimen'', ''undernemen'' (pret. ''undernam'', ''undernom'', pp. ''undernumen'', ''undernomen'', ''undirnomen''), < AS. ''underniman'' (= OHG. ''untarneman'', MHG. ''undernemen'', G. ''unternehmen''), undertake, perceive, < ''under'', under, + ''niman'', take: see ''nim''. Cf. ''underfang'', ''underget'', ''undertake''.] '''1.''' To take; undertake.
{{smaller block|We beoth hider come and this fiht habbeth ''ondernome''.
{{right|''Layamon'', l. 26734.}}}}
'''2.''' To receive; feel; perceive.
{{smaller block|<poem>He the savour ''undernom''
Which that the roses and the lilies caste.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Second Nun’s Tale, l. 243.}}}}
'''3.''' To take up; reprove; reproach.
{{smaller block|Inpacient is he that wol nat ben ytaught ne ''undernome'' of his vice.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Parson’s Tale.}}
Who-so ''vndernymeth'' me here-of I hat hym dedly after.
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), v. 115.}}}}

'''undernote''' (un′dėr-nōt), ''n.'' A low or subdued note; an undertone.
{{smaller block|How every pause is filled with ''undernotes''.
{{right|''Shelley'', Prometheus Unbound, iv. 1.}}}}

'''undernoted''' (un′dėr-nō″ted), ''a.'' Noted below or beneath: as, the ''undernoted'' quantities.

'''undern-song†''', ''n.'' An office sung at undern, or nine o’clock in the morning. ''Rock.''

'''underntime†''', ''n.'' See ''undertime''.

'''underpart''' (un-dėr-pärt′), ''v. t.'' To divide (a part) and assign subordinate portions of it. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Then one part
Is ''under-parted'' to a couple of clerks.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Staple of News, i. 2.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
